topic: Day 1 · Resuscitation & Transfusion — The Restrictive Strategy
speakerAffiliation: Virtual Teaching Hospital · Blood Sciences & Major Haemorrhage Service
speakerBio: A transfusion physician who runs the hospital's major haemorrhage protocol and spends half his life stopping well-meaning teams from over-transfusing. He keeps a framed copy of Villanueva's Kaplan–Meier curve on his office wall.
lectureHTML:
🎯 Where we start — the well-meant unit of blood

Our cirrhotic from Session 1 is now in the bay, resuscitated, HR 96, BP 108/70. His Hb comes back at 78. The instinct of every doctor in the room is the same: "he's bled, give him blood — get him back to normal." A junior prescribes three units to "top him up to 100+." That instinct, applied to this patient, can kill him. This session is about the most counterintuitive lesson in the whole of GI bleeding: when it comes to transfusion, less is more, and the evidence for it is one of the cleanest trials in gastroenterology.

1 · The one sentence that holds the whole topic

In GI bleeding, transfuse to a haemoglobin of 70 g/L, not to normal. The restrictive strategy saves lives — chasing a normal Hb harms them.

For decades we transfused liberally, aiming to restore haemoglobin toward normal. It felt right. It was wrong. The turning point was a single randomised trial that reversed practice worldwide — and the mechanism behind it, especially in cirrhosis, is beautiful once you see it.

2 · The landmark — Villanueva, NEJM 2013 📊

Villanueva et al., "Transfusion Strategies for Acute Upper Gastrointestinal Bleeding," NEJM 2013. A single-centre RCT of 921 patients with acute upper GI bleeding, randomised to:

Restrictive strategyLiberal strategy
Transfusion triggerTransfuse when Hb < 70 g/LTransfuse when Hb < 90 g/L
Target rangeHb 70–90 g/LHb 90–110 g/L
6-week survival95%91%
Further bleeding10%16%
Adverse events / transfusion reactionsLowerHigher

The punchline: the restrictive group had significantly better survival (hazard ratio for death ~0.55), less rebleeding, fewer complications, and used far less blood. Mortality and rebleeding were both reduced by giving less blood. This is the study that made "Hb 70" the default threshold in every modern guideline (ACG 2021, NICE, Baveno VII).

💡 One-liner

"Seventy is plenty." In the haemodynamically stable GI bleeder, hold your hand at a transfusion threshold of Hb 70 g/L and a target of 70–90. The urge to "top up to normal" is the urge that increases death.

3 · WHY less is more — the mechanism, especially in cirrhosis ⚙️

Why should giving blood — the very thing the patient has lost — cause more rebleeding and death? The answer is a vicious cycle, and it is most vivid in the cirrhotic with varices.

The benefit was most pronounced in patients with cirrhosis (Child–Pugh A and B), and here is the physiology:

  1. Varices exist because of portal hypertension. The pressure gradient across the varix wall (the hepatic venous pressure gradient, HVPG) is what drives bleeding. Above an HVPG of ~12 mmHg, varices can bleed; the higher the pressure, the more they bleed.
  2. Transfusion expands the intravascular volume. Pouring blood and volume into the splanchnic circulation raises portal venous pressure — a "portal-pressure rebound."
  3. Rising portal pressure re-stresses the varix. The higher transmural pressure pops a clot that had formed, or bursts a varix that had tamponaded — provoking rebleeding.
  4. Rebleeding worsens everything. More blood loss → more transfusion → more portal pressure → more bleeding. The liberal strategy feeds its own vicious cycle.
In the cirrhotic, over-transfusion raises portal pressure and reopens the varix you just stopped. Restraint keeps the portal system decompressed. Less blood, lower pressure, less rebleeding.
🎯 Contrast — restrictive vs liberal

Restrictive (Hb 70 trigger, 70–90 target): better survival, less rebleeding, lower portal pressure, fewer transfusion reactions and volume-overload events, less demand on the blood bank. Liberal (Hb 90 trigger, 90–110 target): raises portal pressure (rebleeding), increases circulatory overload (TACO), transfusion reactions and immunomodulation, and — counterintuitively — increases mortality. The default in the stable patient is always restrictive.

4 · The exceptions — when 70 is not the number ⚠️

The restrictive threshold governs the stable patient. Physiology overrides the protocol in two settings:

SituationThreshold / approachWhy
Active massive / exsanguinating bleeding, haemodynamic instabilityDo NOT wait for a lab Hb — activate the major haemorrhage protocol and give blood empirically to maintain perfusionIn torrential loss the measured Hb lags reality; the patient is dying of volume, not of a number. The trial excluded the exsanguinating patient.
Acute coronary syndrome / significant ischaemic heart diseaseHigher threshold, target Hb around 80 g/L (some use ~80–100)The ischaemic myocardium tolerates anaemia poorly; oxygen delivery to a stenosed coronary bed matters more than portal pressure. Balance is individualised.
⚠️ Danger — do not apply "Hb 70" to the crashing patient

A patient exsanguinating in front of you does not have a meaningful "current haemoglobin" — you are chasing a lab value from ten minutes and a litre of blood ago. In active massive haemorrhage, transfuse to perfusion and clinical response under the major haemorrhage protocol, not to a threshold. The restrictive rule is for the stabilised patient, not the arrest.

5 · The major haemorrhage protocol — when the tap is open 🚨

When bleeding is massive (roughly: loss of one blood volume in 24h, or half a blood volume in 3h, or ongoing loss with instability), you switch from "component by number" to a pre-defined massive haemorrhage protocol (MHP): fixed packs of blood products delivered rapidly while you fight the source.

  • Ratio-based resuscitation. Give red cells with plasma (FFP) and platelets in a balanced ratio (aim ~1:1:1 for RBC:FFP:platelets) to avoid a dilutional coagulopathy — replacing red cells alone dilutes clotting factors and platelets and makes bleeding worse.
  • Avoid crystalloid over-load. Large-volume crystalloid dilutes clotting factors, drops temperature, and worsens the coagulopathy — give blood, not litres of saline.
  • Call the haematologist / activate the pack early. The lab needs a head start.

The individual products and their targets

ProductWhat it replacesTypical target / trigger
Packed red cellsOxygen-carrying capacityHb ≥ 70 (≥ 80 if IHD); to perfusion if massive
PlateletsPrimary haemostasisTransfuse to keep platelets > 50 ×10⁹/L in active bleeding (>100 if CNS bleed)
Fresh frozen plasma (FFP)All clotting factorsFor deranged coagulation (PT/APTT > 1.5× normal) or as part of the MHP ratio
Fibrinogen / cryoprecipitateFibrinogen specificallyKeep fibrinogen > 1.5 g/L in major bleeding (cryoprecipitate or fibrinogen concentrate)
💡 Pearl — fibrinogen is the first factor to fail

In major haemorrhage, fibrinogen falls to critical levels before other clotting factors. Don't forget to check it and replace it (cryoprecipitate or fibrinogen concentrate) to keep it > 1.5 g/L. A patient who keeps oozing despite red cells and FFP is often fibrinogen-depleted.

6 · Tranexamic acid — the intuitive drug that failed 🧪

Tranexamic acid (TXA) is an antifibrinolytic — it stabilises clot by blocking plasmin. It saves lives in trauma (CRASH-2) and postpartum haemorrhage (WOMAN). So surely it helps GI bleeding? It was used reflexively for years. Then came the definitive trial.

⚠️ Danger — HALT-IT: do NOT routinely give TXA in GI bleeding

HALT-IT (Lancet 2020) randomised over 12,000 patients with acute GI bleeding to high-dose tranexamic acid vs placebo. The result was unambiguous: NO reduction in death from bleeding, and a significant increase in venous thromboembolic events (DVT/PE) and seizures. TXA does not help the GI bleeder and it harms some. Do not routinely use tranexamic acid in acute GI bleeding. This is a clean example of why a mechanism that "should" work must still be tested — the gut is not the uterus.

CRASH-2 and WOMAN made TXA a reflex. HALT-IT took it back for the gut: same drug, different organ, no benefit, more clots.

7 · Reversing anticoagulation — the bleeding patient on blood-thinners 💊

An increasing share of GI bleeders are anticoagulated. Reversal is targeted to the drug — know these cold:

AnticoagulantReversalNotes
Warfarin (vitamin K antagonist)Prothrombin complex concentrate (PCC) + IV vitamin K (5–10 mg)PCC works in minutes and is preferred over FFP for major bleeding; vitamin K sustains reversal. FFP is slower and volume-heavy — second line.
Dabigatran (direct thrombin inhibitor)Idarucizumab (specific monoclonal antibody)Rapid, complete reversal. Consider PCC if unavailable.
Factor Xa inhibitors (apixaban, rivaroxaban)Andexanet alfa (specific), or PCC if unavailableAndexanet is licensed but costly and access-limited; PCC is the widely used pragmatic option.
Heparin (unfractionated)Protamine sulfatePartial reversal for LMWH.
🎯 Key concept — reverse, but weigh the indication

Always ask why the patient is anticoagulated (metallic valve, recent PE, AF) — reversing a metallic mitral valve carries a thrombotic price. In life-threatening GI bleeding, controlling the haemorrhage takes priority, but the decision to restart, and when, is a genuine risk–benefit judgement made with the responsible team.

8 · The harm of over-transfusion — naming the damage 🩸

Blood is a transplant, not a tonic. Every unit carries risk, and giving units the patient does not need is an active harm:

  • Portal-pressure rebound → variceal rebleeding (the cirrhotic mechanism above).
  • TACO — transfusion-associated circulatory overload — pulmonary oedema from volume, a leading cause of transfusion death.
  • TRALI — transfusion-related acute lung injury.
  • Transfusion reactions — febrile, allergic, haemolytic; alloimmunisation.
  • Immunomodulation and infection risk; finite, precious resource stewardship.
☠️ M&M — "We topped him up to 110"

A 58-year-old man with alcohol-related cirrhosis presented with a variceal bleed. Endoscopy banded the varices successfully; post-procedure his Hb was 76 and he was haemodynamically stable. The night team, uneasy at a "low" number, transfused three units to bring his Hb to 112 "to give him some reserve." Four hours later he had a large fresh haematemesis and became hypotensive — the transfusion had raised his portal pressure and blown a banded varix. He needed emergency re-scoping, a Sengstaken–Blakemore tube, and ITU. Review noted the transfusion was given against the restrictive threshold, in a stable patient, and directly precipitated the rebleed. Lessons: (1) In a stable GI bleeder, Hb 70 is the trigger, 70–90 the target — 76 needed no blood. (2) Over-transfusion in cirrhosis raises portal pressure and reopens varices. (3) "Reserve" is a feeling, not an indication. Villanueva was written for exactly this patient.

9 · Take-home 🎯

  • Restrictive wins: transfuse at Hb < 70, target 70–90 (Villanueva NEJM 2013 — better survival, less rebleeding).
  • The benefit is greatest in cirrhosis — over-transfusion raises portal pressure and reopens varices.
  • Exceptions: active massive bleeding → transfuse to perfusion via the major haemorrhage protocol; ischaemic heart disease → target ~80.
  • Massive haemorrhage: balanced ratios (~1:1:1), platelets > 50, fibrinogen > 1.5 g/L, avoid crystalloid overload and hypothermia.
  • Do NOT routinely give tranexamic acid — HALT-IT showed no benefit and more VTE and seizures.
  • Reverse anticoagulants specifically: warfarin → PCC + vitamin K; dabigatran → idarucizumab; Xa inhibitors → andexanet or PCC.
  • Blood is a transplant, not a tonic — over-transfusion causes rebleeding, TACO, TRALI. Seventy is plenty.

Next session: now that the patient is resuscitated and transfused correctly, who is actually safe? The scores that decide who goes home and who needs an urgent scope — Blatchford, Rockall, AIMS65.

moderatorQs.q: Villanueva 2013 found that a restrictive transfusion strategy improved survival, and the benefit was greatest in cirrhotics. Walk us through the mechanism.
moderatorQs.answerHTML: In cirrhosis, varices bleed because of portal hypertension — the transmural pressure across the varix wall (driven by the hepatic venous pressure gradient) is what ruptures it. When you transfuse liberally you expand the intravascular and splanchnic volume, which raises portal venous pressure — a 'portal-pressure rebound.' That rising pressure re-stresses the varix, pops the clot that had formed, and precipitates rebleeding, which begets more transfusion and more pressure in a vicious cycle. The restrictive strategy (transfuse only below Hb 70, target 70–90) keeps the portal system relatively decompressed, so there is less rebleeding and better survival — Villanueva showed ~95% vs 91% six-week survival and 10% vs 16% rebleeding, with the largest benefit in Child–Pugh A/B cirrhotics. Less blood, lower portal pressure, fewer blown varices.

moderatorQs.q: Tranexamic acid saves lives in trauma and postpartum haemorrhage. Why do we NOT give it routinely in GI bleeding?
moderatorQs.answerHTML: Because it was tested and it failed. HALT-IT (Lancet 2020), a randomised trial of over 12,000 patients with acute GI bleeding, found that high-dose tranexamic acid produced no reduction in death from bleeding and caused a significant excess of venous thromboembolism (DVT/PE) and seizures. This is a lesson in not extrapolating mechanism across contexts: CRASH-2 (trauma) and WOMAN (PPH) showed benefit, but the GI tract is a different bleeding environment — much of the fibrinolysis is local and the patient population is older with more thrombotic risk (including cirrhotics). Same drug, different organ, no benefit, more harm — so TXA is not part of routine GI bleeding management.

moderatorQs.q: A patient on apixaban for atrial fibrillation presents with a major upper GI bleed. How do you reverse them, and what if the specific agent isn't available?
moderatorQs.answerHTML: Apixaban is a factor Xa inhibitor, so the specific reversal agent is andexanet alfa, a recombinant decoy Xa that sequesters the drug. However, andexanet is expensive and not universally stocked, so in practice most centres reverse life-threatening Xa-inhibitor bleeding with prothrombin complex concentrate (PCC), which replaces the vitamin-K-dependent factors and restores thrombin generation. You would also stop the drug, note the timing of the last dose and renal function (which affects clearance), give supportive transfusion to targets, and control the source endoscopically. Contrast with dabigatran (a thrombin inhibitor), which has its own specific antidote, idarucizumab, and warfarin, reversed with PCC plus IV vitamin K. Always weigh the thrombotic indication before and after reversal.

audienceQs.q: A stable post-endoscopy patient has an Hb of 76 and the night doctor wants to give two units 'to be safe.' Is that reasonable?
audienceQs.answerHTML: No — and it is exactly the scenario Villanueva warns against. In a haemodynamically stable GI bleeder the transfusion trigger is Hb < 70 g/L with a target of 70–90; an Hb of 76 is above the threshold and needs no blood. 'To be safe' or 'to give reserve' is a feeling, not an indication — and in a cirrhotic it is actively dangerous, because the extra volume raises portal pressure and can reopen a banded or clotted varix, causing rebleeding. Over-transfusion also risks circulatory overload (TACO) and transfusion reactions. The correct plan is to monitor, recheck the Hb, and hold transfusion unless it falls below 70 or the patient becomes unstable or has significant ischaemic heart disease (where the target rises to ~80).

audienceQs.q: When the major haemorrhage protocol is running, why do we give FFP and platelets alongside red cells instead of just red cells and crystalloid?
audienceQs.answerHTML: Because replacing red cells alone — or worse, red cells plus large-volume crystalloid — produces a dilutional coagulopathy: you dilute the clotting factors and platelets the patient needs to actually stop bleeding, and crystalloid also drops their temperature and pH, further impairing clot formation (the 'bloody vicious cycle' of coagulopathy, acidosis and hypothermia). Balanced ratio-based resuscitation (~1:1:1 red cells:FFP:platelets) replaces the whole of what is being lost, keeps platelets > 50 ×10⁹/L and fibrinogen > 1.5 g/L (cryoprecipitate/fibrinogen concentrate — remember fibrinogen falls first), and keeps the patient warm. You give blood, not litres of saline, and you activate the protocol early so the lab can keep up.

audienceQs.q: If the patient is exsanguinating in front of me, do I still wait for the Hb to drop below 70 before transfusing?
audienceQs.answerHTML: No — the restrictive Hb-70 threshold is for the stabilised patient, not the one actively exsanguinating. In torrential, life-threatening haemorrhage the measured haemoglobin lags reality — it reflects blood from ten minutes ago, before the last litre was lost, because in acute whole-blood loss the concentration stays normal until dilution occurs. So in a haemodynamically unstable, actively bleeding patient you activate the major haemorrhage protocol and transfuse empirically to maintain perfusion and clinical response, not to a lab number. Villanueva deliberately excluded exsanguinating patients. Once the bleeding is controlled and the patient is stabilised, you revert to the restrictive Hb-70 trigger.
